Meta da aula. Ao final das quatro sessõe: Lesson goal. By the end of the four sessions, you learn every noun together with its article and plural, spot gender from clues, and use ein/eine and der/die/das — even though English gets by with just "the" and "a".

PASSO 1: O português não tem neutro. O a: STEP 1: English has one word for "the". German has three, one per gender: der (masculine), die (feminine) and das (neuter). In the plural, it's always die. STEP 2: English calls every object "it". German doesn't: a thing is «er», «sie» or «es» depending on its gender — «Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist modern.» STEP 3: so never learn Tisch. Learn der Tisch.
O gênero do alemão não acompanha o do po: Old English had genders too — modern English dropped them, German kept them. That's why the gender of a German noun can't be guessed from its meaning: a table is masculine, a lamp feminine, a girl («das Mädchen») neuter. The gender is part of the word, and the only safe way is to learn it together with the word, as one unit.
Der, die, das: os três gêneros: Der, die, das: the three genders
Em alemão todo substantivo tem gênero: m: In German every noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). Gender is grammar, not meaning: «das Mädchen» (the girl) is neuter. So always memorize the article with the word. EVERY noun is written with a CAPITAL letter, anywhere in the sentence — not just names, as in English. Endings give clues, with exceptions: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion, -ie and most words in -e are feminine; -er, -ling and -ismus are masculine; -chen, -lein, -um and -ment are neuter. Days of the week, months and seasons are masculine. Handy English link: -heit and -schaft often match English -hood and -ship (die Kindheit = childhood, die Freundschaft = friendship).
o português também tem masculino e femin: English only keeps gender in he/she/it for people and animals. German assigns a gender to every noun, and it rarely matches what you'd expect: «das Kind» (the child) is neuter, «die Person» is feminine even for a man.
Kind é neutro e o substantivo leva maiús: Kind is neuter, and nouns are capitalized.

O plural alemão se forma de cinco jeitos: German plurals come in five patterns: -e (der Tisch → die Tische), -(e)n (die Lampe → die Lampen), -er (das Buch → die Bücher), no ending (der Lehrer → die Lehrer) and -s (das Auto → die Autos, common in foreign words). Many words also add an umlaut to the vowel (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü) — just like English man → men, foot → feet, mouse → mice, which are leftovers of the same old Germanic rule. There's no safe rule: learn the plural with the noun. The plural definite article is always «die», for all three genders.
o plural português quase sempre é um «-s: The English reflex is to add -s. In German, -s is the rarest pattern (mostly foreign words: Autos, Hotels). English already has the German patterns in its oldest words: child → children is the German -er (Kind → Kinder), ox → oxen is -en, man → men is the umlaut (Mann → Männer).

«Ein» e «eine» são o «um» e a «uma»: ein: «Ein» and «eine» are the German "a/an": ein Mann, eine Frau, ein Kind. Half the guesswork disappears with one rule: «ein» is for der and das words, «eine» only for die words. As in English, there's no "a" in the plural: «Das sind Bücher» (those are books). To negate a noun, German uses «kein» (or «keine»), with the same endings as «ein»: «Das ist kein Tisch» = "that's not a table" / "that's no table". To point at things, use «das ist» for one and «das sind» for several — «das» here works like English "that", whatever the gender.
There's no "a" in the plural, just like in English.

Introduza o objeto com artigo indefinido: Introduce the object with "a" (ein/eine): Das ist ___ Bett. → Das Bett ist alt.
Bett é neutro. O artigo indefinido no no: Bett is neuter, so "a" is ein: ein Bett.
